description: A social and cultural anthropologist whose work connects exchange, migration and the cultural dimensions of globalization. He examines how circulation produces value and how moving people maintain and transform identities, rather than treating cultures as bounded, static wholes.

sources.note: New limited rereading: publisher summary and first primary paragraph on Simmel, exchange and the political creation of value; metadata names Appadurai as chapter author and volume editor, print 1986. The online 2014 date is distinct. Remaining chapter and other contributors unread. Earlier qualification retained.

description: A cultural theorist and historian of racialized modernity, Black British life and Atlantic diaspora. His Black Atlantic framework crosses national boundaries and treats slavery, music and double consciousness as central to modernity while resisting closed racial identities.
classification_flag: UCL explicitly describes political/cultural and global historical research alongside critical theory. Assigned theory resource placement retained for this packet; no departmental exclusion or automatic reclassification.

sources.note: New rereading: title/contents and complete preface ix–xi. description: A sociologist whose work makes collective institutions, obligations and representations objects of causal inquiry. His methodological writings distinguish external and constraining social facts from their mere frequency, and distinguish the causes of institutions from the functions they later serve.

sources.note: New limited rereading through linked Wikisource Chapitre_1 opening (external obligations, coercion, signs and social currents) and Chapitre_5 section I opening (cause/function distinction, survivals and changed uses). Consulted 1919 Alcan witness, not an original-edition collation. Remaining chapters unread in this pass; prior broader passage qualifications retained.

description: The founder of psychoanalysis, whose accounts of unconscious processes, identification and group bonds became resources for historical interpretation. Historical use requires evidence about social settings as well as psychological hypotheses; Peter Gay explicitly warns against reducing historical explanation to psychoanalysis.

sources.note: New rereading: title, translator’s note and complete chapter I, printed pp. 1–4. German original 1921 and James Strachey English translation 1922 kept distinct; note records author-requested relocation of passages into footnotes. Chapter IV was read in the earlier accepted source review, but not newly reread here; remaining chapters unread. Universal and clinical claims not independently verified.

sources.note: Complete question/answer defining psychohistory read: Gay prefers a historian oriented toward psychoanalysis and treats it as an auxiliary discipline, rejecting reductionism and insisting on the external world and evidence. Other interview answers not fully read. Direct requests denied but browser text accessible. Gay’s evaluative remarks about Freud as historian are his judgments, not atlas facts.

description: A political scientist whose development arguments distinguish political institutionalization from economic growth and electoral form. His later civilizational model remains a subject of controversy; Edward Said criticized its treatment of internally diverse societies as coherent opposing civilizations.

sources.note: New limited rereading of title/imprint and complete printed p. 1. Original copyright 1968, consulted seventh printing 1973. Distinction between forms and degree/capacity of government read directly; later pages not newly read completely. Earlier 1–7 and 12–13 review and its country-judgment/order-first qualifications preserved.

description: A philosopher of sovereignty, law and forms of life whose Homo sacer project uses historical paradigms to examine political structures. In his own account, the state of exception connects law with anomy; he distinguishes this paradigmatic method from a comprehensive historical survey.

sources.note: Complete interview pp. 609–614 including editorial notes read. Conversation Rome 4 March 2004; German Süddeutsche Zeitung publication 6 April; English translation Morag Goodwin. Agamben explicitly distinguishes paradigmatic method from being a historian and names Foucault’s panopticon/archaeology as resources. Editor notes are distinct from answers. Incidental 1968 Collège course and 1934 Nuremberg-law dates are erroneous and not adopted; policy/historical generalizations are attributed, not independently established. Books unread.

description: A philosopher, social theorist and critic of music and mass culture associated with the Frankfurt School. With Max Horkheimer he linked standardized cultural production to concentrated economic power; their treatment of amusement and the split between light and serious art complicates a simple opposition between commerce and autonomous culture.

sources.note: New limited rereading: opening from the sociological theory of cultural chaos through standardization, economic power and technology; later selected paragraphs from Amusement and all the elements through the high/light-art division and amusement as a prolongation of work. Intervening and later body unread. Joint Horkheimer/Adorno authorship and host’s missing precise English-edition/translator retained; generalizations remain attributed arguments.
